I have developed the following projects:

1️⃣ TELEGRAM BOT FOR ENGINEERING STUDENTS: Designed and deployed a bot that helps students access subject materials seamlessly.

2️⃣ HOSTEL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM: Developed using Java (NetBeans), this system efficiently manages data related to students and hostel workers.

3️⃣ COURSE AUTOMATION AI AGENT – FULL STACK WEB DEVELOPMENT: Built an AI-powered platform that emails daily course content based on user schedules and generates beginner-friendly lessons with PDF certificates upon completion.

4️⃣ COLLEGE FEE QUEUE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM: Developed a smart queue management platform that reduces student waiting time by allowing them to join fee counters online, view their queue position, and get real-time updates — improving efficiency and user experience.

I am passionate about turning ideas into innovations through technology. 🚀

🚀 Day 20 of My Daily DSA Practice Journey 💻🔥
Today marks Day 20 of staying consistent with my Data Structures & Algorithms practice, and this session was all about Recursion, Mathematical Optimization, and Problem-Solving Patterns.
Problems solved today:
🔹 Fibonacci Number
🔹 Pow(x, n)
🔹 Count Good Numbers
🔹 Valid Palindrome (Recursion)
These problems may look simple at first glance, but they helped me strengthen some very important concepts that are frequently used in coding interviews and competitive programming.
📌 Fibonacci Number
Revised the classic recursion pattern.
Understood why the naive recursive solution has exponential complexity.
Compared recursion with memoization and iterative approaches.
📌 Pow(x, n)
Practiced Binary Exponentiation (Fast Power).
Learned how to reduce the time complexity from O(n) to O(log n).
Understood how recursion can be combined with divide-and-conquer for efficient computation.
Also explored handling of negative powers and integer overflow edge cases.
📌 Count Good Numbers
Applied modular arithmetic and recursive fast exponentiation.
Learned how mathematical observations can simplify a problem significantly.
Realized the importance of using long and modulo operations carefully when dealing with very large numbers.
📌 Valid Palindrome (Recursion)
Practiced the two-pointer recursive pattern.
Improved my understanding of recursive base cases and termination conditions.
Learned how recursion can elegantly replace iterative pointer movement.
What I focused on today:
✔️ Writing clean recursive functions
✔️ Designing correct base cases
✔️ Understanding recursion stack behavior
✔️ Avoiding StackOverflowError
✔️ Handling overflow using long
✔️ Analyzing time and space complexity before coding
One important realization from today’s practice:
👉 Recursion is not just repeatedly calling the same function. The real challenge is identifying the correct recursive state, reducing the problem size in every call, and ensuring that the recursion always moves toward a valid base case.
This journey is teaching me much more than coding:
How to break down complex problems.
How to think about edge cases before implementation.
How to debug recursive solutions systematically.
And most importantly, how consistency compounds over time.
📊 Day 20 Progress
✅ 4 problems solved
✅ Recursion fundamentals strengthened
✅ Binary Exponentiation mastered
✅ Modular arithmetic practiced
✅ Better understanding of recursive debugging and optimization
I’m excited to continue this journey and move toward more advanced topics like Merge Sort-based counting problems, Divide & Conquer, Backtracking, and Dynamic Programming in the coming days.
Every day of practice is a small step toward becoming a better problem solver and software engineer. 💪
#Day20 #DSA #Recursion #Java #LeetCode #BinaryExponentiation #ModularArithmetic #ProblemSolving #CodingJourney #SoftwareEngineering #Programming #DataStructures #Algorithms #100DaysOfCode #TechJourney

🚀 Day 18 & Day 19 of my  Daily DSA Practice Journey
Over the last two days, I focused on mastering the Two Pointers pattern and advanced array optimization techniques.
Problems solved:
✅ 167. Two Sum II – Input Array Is Sorted
✅ 80. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
✅ 977. Squares of a Sorted Array
✅ 15. 3Sum
✅ 16. 3Sum Closest
✅ 581. Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
✅ 75. Sort Colors
Key learnings:
🔹 Using two pointers to optimize sorted-array problems from O(n²) to O(n).
🔹 Performing in-place array modifications with O(1) extra space.
🔹 Fixing one element and applying two pointers to solve 3Sum efficiently while handling duplicates carefully.
🔹 Understanding prefix maximum & suffix minimum scanning to find the shortest unsorted subarray in linear time.
🔹 Applying the Dutch National Flag algorithm for sorting 0s, 1s, and 2s without using a sorting library.
🔹 Improving my ability to identify the correct pattern before coding, which makes optimization much easier.
Patterns practiced:
📌 Two Pointers
📌 In-place Array Manipulation
📌 Prefix/Suffix Scanning
📌 Dutch National Flag Algorithm
📌 Greedy Array Traversal
One important realization from these problems is that pattern recognition is often more valuable than memorizing solutions. Once the right pattern is identified, the implementation becomes much more intuitive and efficient.
Consistency + pattern recognition + optimization mindset = steady progress toward becoming a better problem solver. 💪🔥
#DSA #Java #LeetCode #100DaysOfCode #ProblemSolving #Algorithms #CodingJourney #SoftwareEngineering

Sometimes the best opportunities come when you least expect them.
While casually scrolling through Instagram stories, I came across a post from CHANDAN KUMAR CHERIPALLY Anna, Founder of Repeatless Agency. In the story, he announced a technical challenge and mentioned that two participants would receive direct full-time opportunities.
Honestly, I knew the competition would be intense. There are many talented developers participating, and getting selected is never guaranteed. But one thing I've learned throughout my journey is that opportunities are rarely won by those who hesitate—they are won by those who take action.
So, without overthinking, I accepted the challenge and decided to give it my best effort.
For this assignment, I performed an in-depth analysis of MailMind AI, an AI-powered Gmail intelligence platform. Instead of simply reviewing the project, I explored its architecture, workflows, technology stack, design decisions, and scalability considerations.
Some of the key areas I analyzed included:
🔹 Google OAuth 2.0 Authentication Flow and JWT-based Security
🔹 Spring Boot Backend Architecture with Asynchronous Processing
🔹 Next.js Frontend Architecture and User Experience Design
🔹 Gmail API Integration and Incremental Email Synchronization
🔹 AI-Powered Email Categorization and Summarization
🔹 RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Pipeline for Intelligent Email Search
🔹 PostgreSQL + pgvector for Semantic Search and Embedding Storage
🔹 Google Gemini and NVIDIA NIM Integration Strategy
🔹 Database Design, Performance Optimizations, and System Trade-offs
🔹 Production Scalability Considerations and Future Improvements
What impressed me most was not just the project itself, but the thought process behind the challenge. Instead of relying on traditional hiring methods, Chandan Anna and Repeatless Agency are encouraging people to demonstrate their skills through practical problem-solving and real-world analysis. I genuinely believe this approach helps uncover talent far more effectively than evaluating resumes alone.
Whether I get selected or not, this challenge was already a valuable experience. It gave me an opportunity to study a production-grade AI application, strengthen my system design understanding, and think like an engineer responsible for building scalable software products.
A heartfelt thank you to Chandan Anna and the entire Repeatless Agency team for creating opportunities that inspire developers to learn, build, and challenge themselves.
Excited to see what comes next, and grateful for the learning journey so far. 🚀

🚀 Day 17/45 – #SDESheetChallenge 💻
Another strong day of recursion and backtracking completed ✅
Today’s focus was on:
✔️ Combination Sum
✔️ Unique Combinations
✔️ K-th Permutation Logic
The biggest learning today:
👉 Recursion becomes easier when we clearly understand pick, not-pick, and backtracking.
🔹 Combination Sum
This problem helped me understand the classic pick / not-pick pattern.
Core idea:
✅ Pick the current element
✅ Reduce the target
✅ Stay on the same index because reuse is allowed
✅ Backtrack and explore other possibilities
This problem taught me:
✔️ Recursive decision making
✔️ Backtracking basics
✔️ Reusing elements in combinations
✔️ Target-based recursion
🔹 Combination Sum II
This problem added an important condition:
Each number can be used only once, and duplicate combinations are not allowed.
Approach:
✅ Sort the array
✅ Pick elements one by one
✅ Move to the next index after picking
✅ Skip duplicate elements carefully
This problem taught me:
✔️ Duplicate handling
✔️ Backtracking with constraints
✔️ Pruning unnecessary recursion
✔️ Clean combination generation
🔹 K-th Permutation Sequence
This was a very interesting mathematical problem 🔥
Instead of generating all permutations, the optimal approach uses factorial logic.
Core idea:
✅ Convert K to 0-based indexing
✅ Divide permutations into factorial blocks
✅ Pick the correct digit for each position
✅ Remove used digits and continue
This problem taught me:
✔️ Factorial-based indexing
✔️ Permutation block logic
✔️ Avoiding brute-force generation
✔️ Mathematical optimization
💡 Major Learnings from Day 17:
✅ Backtracking is about exploring and undoing choices
✅ Sorting helps avoid duplicate combinations
✅ Pick / not-pick is a powerful recursion pattern
✅ Factorials help directly find permutation positions
✅ Optimization comes from understanding the pattern deeply
Consistency continues… 🚀
Excited for Day 18 🔥

🚀 Day 16/45 – #SDESheetChallenge 💻
Another strong day of problem solving completed ✅
Today’s focus was on:
✔️ Dynamic Programming
✔️ Greedy Strategy
✔️ Recursion & Backtracking
The biggest learning today:
👉 Some problems look greedy at first, but only DP can guarantee the correct answer.
🔹 Minimum Coins
Started by understanding why greedy does not always work.
Example:
For coins [1, 5, 6, 9] and target 11, greedy picks:
➡️ 9 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins
But the optimal answer is:
✅ 5 + 6 = 2 coins
Then explored:
✅ Memoization
✅ Tabulation
✅ Space Optimization
This problem taught me:
✔️ Pick / Not Pick DP pattern
✔️ Overlapping subproblems
✔️ Minimum-value DP thinking
✔️ Why greedy fails in some cases
🔹 Assign Cookies
This was a clean greedy problem.
Core idea:
Give the smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy child.
Approach:
✅ Sort students
✅ Sort cookies
✅ Use two pointers
If the cookie satisfies the child, move both pointers.
If not, try a bigger cookie.
This problem taught me:
✔️ Greedy matching
✔️ Sorting-based optimization
✔️ Two pointer usage
✔️ Maximizing satisfied children efficiently
🔹 Subset Sum – Sum of All Subsets
Started with the bitmasking approach where every subset is represented using binary choices.
Then learned the recursive approach:
✅ Include the current element
✅ Exclude the current element
✅ Store the sum when recursion reaches the end
This problem taught me:
✔️ Subset generation
✔️ Recursion tree thinking
✔️ Include / Exclude pattern
✔️ Generating all possible outcomes
🔹 Subset II – Unique Subsets
This problem added an important twist: duplicates.
Brute force approach:
➡️ Generate all subsets
➡️ Store them in a set to remove duplicates
Optimal approach:
✅ Sort the array first
✅ Use backtracking
✅ Skip duplicates during recursion itself
This problem taught me:
✔️ Backtracking with duplicate handling
✔️ Pruning unnecessary calls
✔️ Unique subset generation
✔️ Clean recursive problem solving
💡 Major Learnings from Day 16:
✅ DP is needed when greedy choices fail
✅ Sorting helps greedy and backtracking problems
✅ Recursion becomes easier with include/exclude thinking
✅ Duplicate handling should be done during generation
✅ Backtracking builds strong problem-solving intuition
Every day of this challenge is improving my confidence in solving different patterns step by step.
Consistency continues… 🚀
Excited for Day 17 🔥
